input_signals.name: Industry Sales Yield With Margin Improvement
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(revt, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_RANK(TREND(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at), 5)))
input_signals.hypothesis: A low price-to-sales relative to industry peers predicts returns only when gross profitability is trending up; when margins are deteriorating the depressed sales multiple correctly prices a decaying franchise.
input_signals.reasoning: Sales-to-price is the valuation multiple least contaminated by accounting choices, and the five-year gross-profitability trend supplies a directional quality state that separates recovering cheap firms from structurally impaired ones. Both legs are industry-ranked so the interaction is measured within peer groups, avoiding a mechanical sector bet toward low-margin industries.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( ratio( revt, mul( prcc_f, csho ) ) ), ind_rank( trend( ratio( sub( revt, cogs ), at ), 5 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Solvency-Gated Enterprise Earnings Yield
input_signals.expression: MUL(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(ebitda, MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 1)), MUL(INDICATOR(RATIO(re, at), 0), INDICATOR(NEG(RATIO(SUB(ADD(dltt, dlc), che), at)), -0.3)))
input_signals.hypothesis: A high operating earnings yield is evidence of mispricing only for firms that can survive to realize it; if retained earnings are negative or net debt is large relative to assets, the low price is compensation for solvency risk rather than a mispricing, so the valuation signal should be switched off entirely.
input_signals.reasoning: This replaces the earlier additive rank average with an explicit multiplicative gate: the quality/solvency variables no longer contribute their own return premium at all, they only decide whether the valuation signal is transmitted, which is exactly the conditional language of the hypothesis. It is the mirror image of Signal 1 (there valuation gates quality, here solvency gates valuation), the thresholds are unit-free accounting ratios with non-zero denominators (at), and distressed cheap names are pushed to a neutral zero rather than into the long leg.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( zscore( winsor( ratio( ebitda, mul( prcc_f, csho ) ), 1 ) ), mul( indicator( ratio( re, at ), 0 ), indicator( neg( ratio( sub( add( dltt, dlc ), che ), at ) ), -0.3 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Non-Cash Charge Valuation Wedge
input_signals.expression: SUB(IND_RANK(RATIO(ADD(ib, dp), MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_RANK(RATIO(ib, MUL(prcc_f, csho))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Firms that look far cheaper on cash earnings than on reported net income have earnings depressed by heavy non-cash depreciation charges; that gap is conservative accounting quality, not economic weakness, and the market underprices the hidden cash generation.
input_signals.reasoning: Both legs are valuation ranks, so the spread is close to HML-neutral by construction and its abnormal return cannot come from a simple cheapness bet — the only surviving content is the depreciation wedge, which FF5 does not price. Industry ranking prevents the signal from becoming a pure capital-intensity sector tilt, and the difference form avoids the doubly-bad-corner problem of rank products.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: sub( ind_rank( ratio( add( ib, dp ), mul( prcc_f, csho ) ) ), ind_rank( ratio( ib, mul( prcc_f, csho ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Glamour With Working-Capital Bloat
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(NEG(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), MUL(prcc_f, csho)))), IND_RANK(DELTA(RATIO(SUB(act, lct), at), 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: The sharpest valuation-quality mispricing sits on the overpriced side: firms carrying a rich price relative to the gross profit they actually generate, while simultaneously inflating net working capital, are financing an expensive valuation with soft, reversing accounting numbers and should underperform.
input_signals.reasoning: Rather than swapping a gate inside the same yield×indicator template, this flips the economic side of the interaction: the informative corner is expensive-plus-deteriorating-quality, which is where limits to arbitrage bind hardest and where FF5's HML and RMW have the least power because both legs are ranked within industry. Using NEG of the gross-profit yield rather than the inverted multiple keeps negative-gross-profit firms at the expensive extreme instead of flipping their sign, and the product of two non-negative industry ranks makes the top corner unambiguously the doubly-bad firm.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( neg( ratio( sub( revt, cogs ), mul( prcc_f, csho ) ) ) ), ind_rank( delta( ratio( sub( act, lct ), at ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Multiple Agreement Cheapness
input_signals.expression: MIN(IND_RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), MUL(prcc_f, csho))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Cheapness is credible only when independent accounting bases agree: a firm cheap on book value but expensive on gross profit is an asset-heavy business with no earning power, while a firm cheap on gross profit but expensive on book has already written its assets up; only agreement across both bases identifies genuine underpricing.
input_signals.reasoning: Price appears in both legs and they are combined with a non-linear MIN rather than a difference, so the scaling does not cancel and the construct cannot collapse to gross-profits-to-assets — the object measured is disagreement across multiples, a dimension RMW does not represent. The quality content enters through which fundamental the market is being asked to capitalize (gross profit versus book assets), so the long leg is cheap-and-earning rather than merely cheap.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: min( ind_rank( ratio( ceq, mul( prcc_f, csho ) ) ), ind_rank( ratio( sub( revt, cogs ), mul( prcc_f, csho ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Cheap And Retiring Net Obligations
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_RANK(NEG(DELTA(RATIO(SUB(lt, che), at), 1))))
input_signals.hypothesis: A depressed valuation resolves into returns when the firm is actively shrinking its net obligations: deleveraging transfers enterprise value to equity holders, whereas a cheap firm whose net liabilities keep rising is transferring value to creditors and is a genuine trap.
input_signals.reasoning: This abandons the binary yield×indicator template for a continuous product of two non-negative industry ranks, so no firm is parked at an artificial zero and portfolio composition stays stable across time. The quality channel is the change in cash-netted total obligations rather than a static solvency level or a working-capital accrual, which makes it distinct from both the archived solvency gate and the accrual-based proposals, and only loosely related to CMA's asset-growth content.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( ratio( ceq, mul( prcc_f, csho ) ) ), ind_rank( neg( delta( ratio( sub( lt, che ), at ), 1 ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Net Cash Cheapness With Real Gross Profit
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(che, ADD(dltt, dlc)), MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_RANK(MA(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at), 3)))
input_signals.hypothesis: A large net-cash position relative to market value signals undervaluation only when the firm runs a genuinely profitable operating business; in cash-burning shells the same net-cash yield reflects a melting asset and predicts poor returns, which is why unfiltered net-cash cheapness has a perverse cross-sectional slope.
input_signals.reasoning: It keeps the balance-sheet channel that produced the archive's only positive FF5 alpha but repairs its diagnosed defect by requiring three-year average gross profitability, a persistent quality state that shells cannot fake. Both legs are non-negative industry ranks, so the top corner is unambiguously cash-rich-and-profitable and the bottom corner is levered-and-unprofitable, which is exactly the quality-value versus value-trap partition.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( ratio( sub( che, add( dltt, dlc ) ), mul( prcc_f, csho ) ) ), ind_rank( ma( ratio( sub( revt, cogs ), at ), 3 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Cheapness Amplified By Cash-Backing Persistence
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), MUL(prcc_f, csho))), TS_SUM(INDICATOR(SUB(oancf, ib), 0), 5))
input_signals.hypothesis: What distinguishes quality value is not the level of earnings quality in one year but its repetition: a cheap firm whose operating cash flow has exceeded reported earnings in most of the last five years has demonstrably conservative accounting, while a single clean year is uninformative.
input_signals.reasoning: The quality leg is a persistence count in {0,...,5} rather than a level or a gate, so it amplifies cheapness continuously without creating a zero mass, and habitual conservatism is a state no FF5 factor represents. Pairing it with gross-profit-to-price rather than book-to-market keeps the valuation leg tied to an income statement line that accrual management cannot easily distort.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( ratio( sub( revt, cogs ), mul( prcc_f, csho ) ) ), ts_sum( indicator( sub( oancf, ib ), 0 ), 5 ) )

input_signals.name: Owner Earnings Yield After Working-Capital Funding
input_signals.expression: WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(MA(ADD(ib, dp), 3), MA(DELTA(SUB(act, lct), 1), 3)), MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 1)
input_signals.hypothesis: What an owner can actually take out is cash earnings less the working capital the business must keep funding; a cheap firm whose reported profits are consumed by growing receivables and inventory is a value trap, while a cheap firm whose earnings survive the working-capital charge is genuinely underpriced.
input_signals.reasoning:
Rather than re-ranking an existing archive expression, this changes the numerator's economic content: the quality theme enters by deducting the balance-sheet investment (act, lct) required to sustain earnings, so two firms with identical earnings yields are separated by whether their profits are self-financing. Three-year averaging of both the cash-earnings and the working-capital-investment legs keeps the measure a durable state rather than a one-year accrual reading, and the ratio is monotone with near-universal coverage.
REASONING_END
HYPOTHESIS_END

input_signals.normalized_expression: winsor( ratio( sub( ma( add( ib, dp ), 3 ), ma( delta( sub( act, lct ), 1 ), 3 ) ), mul( prcc_f, csho ) ), 1 )

input_signals.name: Earned Capital Per Dollar Of Total Claims
input_signals.expression: WINSOR(RATIO(re, ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), lt)), 1)
input_signals.hypothesis: Book value that was earned and retained is evidence of a long profit history, whereas book value contributed by investors is not; a firm carrying deep retained earnings relative to the entire stack of claims on it — market equity plus all liabilities — is cheap for quality reasons, while a firm with thin or negative earned capital priced at the same multiple is cheap because it has never generated value.
input_signals.reasoning:
This drops the twice-used yield×quality-rank product for a single monotone ratio in which the quality theme defines the numerator (earned rather than contributed capital) and the valuation theme, together with the obligation stack, defines the denominator, so leverage cannot manufacture apparent cheapness. The denominator is strictly positive, avoiding the sign discontinuities that plagued earlier ratio attempts, coverage is essentially universal, and negative-retained-earnings firms sort to the short leg where the distress story places them.
REASONING_END
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: winsor( ratio( re, add( mul( prcc_f, csho ), lt ) ), 1 )

input_signals.name: Net Cash Cheapness With Liability Coverage
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(che, ADD(dltt, dlc)), MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_RANK(MA(RATIO(oancf, lt), 3)))
input_signals.hypothesis: What makes cash-rich cheapness durable is that the operating business can also service the obligations it does carry; cash-flow coverage of total liabilities, rather than the level of margin, is the quality state that distinguishes a mispriced balance sheet from one whose cash is already spoken for.
input_signals.reasoning: The archive's best signal pairs the net-cash valuation leg with gross-profits-to-assets, a quantity RMW largely spans, so the critic's concern that the profitability leg carries the load is testable by swapping in a solvency-flow quality measure that FF5 does not represent. If the alpha survives or improves, the mispricing is about balance-sheet safety rather than profitability level; if it collapses, the profitability channel was doing the work.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( ratio( sub( che, add( dltt, dlc ) ), mul( prcc_f, csho ) ) ), ind_rank( ma( ratio( oancf, lt ), 3 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Cheapness Backed By Liquid Assets
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_RANK(RATIO(act, at)))
input_signals.hypothesis: A low price-to-book is credible when the book value sits in current assets that can be converted or redeployed, and is suspect when it sits in long-lived operating assets whose carrying value depends on the same weak business the market is discounting; asset composition therefore determines whether book value is a floor or an accounting artifact.
input_signals.reasoning: Asset-composition quality is an untested channel here and is conceptually distinct from profitability, leverage and accruals — it speaks to the reliability of the denominator in the valuation ratio rather than to the income statement. It also offers a cheap, high-coverage test of whether the alpha in the net-cash family generalises to liquidity of the whole asset base rather than cash specifically.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( ratio( ceq, mul( prcc_f, csho ) ) ), ind_rank( ratio( act, at ) ) )

input_signals.name: Cheap With Interest-Free Financing Mix
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_RANK(NEG(RATIO(ADD(dltt, dlc), lt))))
input_signals.hypothesis: What makes a discount dangerous is not the size of a firm's obligations but their type: trade payables and accrued expenses are interest-free, renegotiable financing that reflects supplier bargaining power, whereas interest-bearing debt carries fixed dates that can force liquidation before a mispricing corrects, so cheap firms whose liabilities are predominantly non-financial should realise the value premium.
input_signals.reasoning:
This replaces the incoherent che-minus-lt construction with the obligation *composition* rather than its level, so the quality leg is a bounded share in [0,1] with a clear economic reading and no dependence on cash being large relative to liabilities. It tests a distinct hypothesis from the archive's net-cash signal — that the trap mechanism is the hardness of the claim, not the absence of claims — and the two together identify whether cash buffers or claim softness drive the observed alpha.
REASONING_END
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( ratio( sub( revt, cogs ), mul( prcc_f, csho ) ) ), ind_rank( neg( ratio( add( dltt, dlc ), lt ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Cheap With Compounding Earned Capital Per Share
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_RANK(GROWTH(RATIO(re, csho), 3)))
input_signals.hypothesis: The quality that redeems a low valuation is per-share accumulation of earned capital: a cheap firm whose retained earnings per share have compounded over three years is quietly building shareholder value, while a cheap firm whose earned capital per share is flat or shrinking is either losing money or diluting existing holders to stay funded.
input_signals.reasoning:
Rather than restating the net-external-financing anomaly as a standalone leg, dilution enters only through the per-share denominator of a value-creation measure, so a firm that issues shares while growing earned capital faster still scores well — the signal reads capital creation net of dilution, not issuance itself. This makes the quality state a cumulative outcome variable (retained profit per share) rather than a financing action, which is the conditioning the value-trap story actually requires.
REASONING_END
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( ratio( sub( revt, cogs ), mul( prcc_f, csho ) ) ), ind_rank( growth( ratio( re, csho ), 3 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Net Liquid Claim Cheapness With Gross Profit
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(act, lt), MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_RANK(MA(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at), 3)))
input_signals.hypothesis: The shareholder's hard claim is current assets less every liability — receivables, inventory and cash that could in principle be realised against obligations — and a firm priced low relative to that net liquid claim while still earning gross profit is mispriced rather than distressed.
input_signals.reasoning: This upgrades the valuation leg from cash-versus-financial-debt to the full Graham net-current-asset claim, which unlike the earlier flagged che-minus-lt construction is genuinely two-sided in the cross-section because current assets are of comparable magnitude to total liabilities for most firms. Holding the profitability leg fixed against the archive's net-cash version isolates whether the alpha comes from cash specifically or from any unencumbered liquid claim.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( ratio( sub( act, lt ), mul( prcc_f, csho ) ) ), ind_rank( ma( ratio( sub( revt, cogs ), at ), 3 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Cheapness Backed By Working Liquid Assets
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_RANK(RATIO(revt, act)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Liquid assets support a low valuation only when they are actually turning: receivables that get collected and inventory that sells are convertible value, while a large current-asset balance that generates little revenue is stale inventory and uncollectible receivables that will be written down.
input_signals.reasoning: The archive shows B/M times the *level* of asset liquidity earns positive alpha, but level cannot distinguish convertible working assets from accumulating dead ones; replacing the level with current-asset turnover tests directly which interpretation drives the result. The pair of signals is jointly diagnostic — if turnover works better, the mechanism is realisability of book value, if the level works better, it is balance-sheet safety.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( ratio( ceq, mul( prcc_f, csho ) ) ), ind_rank( ratio( revt, act ) ) )

input_signals.name: Cheapness With A Written-Down Asset Base
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_RANK(RATIO(TS_SUM(dp, 5), at)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Historical-cost accounting understates the value of an old, heavily depreciated asset base, so a firm that is cheap on book value while having charged five years of depreciation large relative to its current assets is cheap against an understated denominator; a firm equally cheap with a freshly capitalised asset base has no such hidden margin.
input_signals.reasoning:
This replaces the enterprise-multiple rediscovery with an accounting-conservatism channel: cumulative depreciation relative to the current asset base is an asset-vintage state, monotone and non-negative for every firm, so there is no sign discontinuity or sparse-tail dependence. The mechanism explains why some low price-to-book firms are genuinely cheap — their book denominator is stale — which is a quality-of-book story rather than a quality-of-earnings story and is not represented in HML, RMW or CMA.
REASONING_END
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( ratio( ceq, mul( prcc_f, csho ) ) ), ind_rank( ratio( ts_sum( dp, 5 ), at ) ) )

input_signals.name: Rank-Weighted Stock And Flow Claim Cheapness
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(SUMRANK(RATIO(SUB(act, lt), MUL(prcc_f, csho)), RATIO(MA(ADD(ib, dp), 3), MUL(prcc_f, csho)))), IND_RANK(MA(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at), 3)))
input_signals.hypothesis: The shareholder's claim is both a stock of unencumbered liquid assets and a recurring stream of cash earnings, and neither should dominate the other by an accident of accounting magnitude; a firm cheap on both components at once, while earning gross profit, is the strongest quality-value case.
input_signals.reasoning:
Combining the two claim components as equally weighted ranks removes the implicit one-times capitalization of the flow term that made the earlier additive version numerically indistinguishable from its balance-sheet leg, so the flow genuinely moves the ordering. This makes the test meaningful: if it beats the archived net-liquid-claim signal, the recurring-cash component adds information the stock claim misses, which is exactly the question the archive leaves open.
REASONING_END
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( sumrank( ratio( sub( act, lt ), mul( prcc_f, csho ) ), ratio( ma( add( ib, dp ), 3 ), mul( prcc_f, csho ) ) ) ), ind_rank( ma( ratio( sub( revt, cogs ), at ), 3 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Cheapness With Operating Cash Runway
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_RANK(RATIO(che, cogs)))
input_signals.hypothesis: A cheap firm realises its value only if it can wait; cash measured against the annual cost of running the business is the firm's survival horizon, and a firm with several quarters of costs in hand never has to issue equity at a depressed price, whereas a firm with weeks of runway must dilute its owners exactly when the discount is widest.
input_signals.reasoning:
Cash scaled by operating costs is a survival-horizon concept rather than a leverage or asset-composition ratio, so it is economically distinct from the liability-intensity and current-asset-share screens the archive has already tested, and it explains *why* liquidity matters for value realisation rather than merely restating that it does. Both inputs are near-universally reported, keeping coverage in the high tier, and the interaction targets the specific mechanism — forced dilution at depressed prices — that converts cheapness into a trap.
REASONING_END

input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( ratio( ceq, mul( prcc_f, csho ) ) ), ind_rank( ratio( che, cogs ) ) )

input_signals.name: Liquid Claim With Trough Profitability
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(act, lt), MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_RANK(TS_MIN(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at), 5)))
input_signals.hypothesis: What separates a quality-value firm from a trap is not its average profitability but its worst year: a cheap, liquid firm that stayed profitable through its own five-year trough has a business that does not break, while one whose current profitability sits above a deeply negative trough is cyclically flattered.
input_signals.reasoning:
Moving the through-cycle minimum from the balance-sheet claim to profitability removes the mechanical correlation with the valuation leg that made the earlier version close to squaring one quantity, while preserving the durability concept the critic judged genuinely novel. It also poses a clean question against the archive, whose profitability screens all use three-year averages: whether the trough or the mean is the informative moment of the quality distribution.
REASONING_END

input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( ratio( sub( act, lt ), mul( prcc_f, csho ) ) ), ind_rank( ts_min( ratio( sub( revt, cogs ), at ), 5 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Claim Cheapness With Survival Horizon

input_signals.hypothesis: A discount is realised by shareholders when the firm owns an unencumbered claim larger than its price and can also fund its operating cost base from cash on hand, because such a firm chooses when to transact rather than being forced by creditors or a cash shortfall.
input_signals.reasoning: This unites the archive's two strongest and economically complementary results — the rank-weighted stock-and-flow claim valuation leg (fmb 5.57, alpha +2.4%) and the operating cash runway quality leg (alpha +2.9%, t 3.21) — which describe the same forced-transaction mechanism from the asset side and the liquidity side respectively. Because the runway leg uses cash against cost of goods sold while the valuation leg uses net current assets against price, the two are far less mechanically entangled than the profitability screens tried previously.

input_signals.name: Cheapness With Cash Beyond Precautionary Need
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_RANK(RATIO(RATIO(che, at), VOL(RATIO(ADD(ib, dp), at), 5))))
input_signals.hypothesis: How much cash a firm needs depends on how uncertain its cash flows are; a cheap firm holding far more cash than its own earnings volatility justifies is carrying an unrecognised distributable asset, whereas the same cash balance in a volatile business is merely a required buffer and adds no value to shareholders.
input_signals.reasoning: This is the one genuinely new mechanism in the batch: it scales the liquidity channel by the firm's own precautionary requirement rather than by its cost base, so it distinguishes excess cash from necessary cash — a distinction no archived signal makes and that the corporate cash-holdings literature says drives the market's valuation of a dollar of cash. The ratio is strictly positive in both numerator and denominator, so it is monotone with no sign discontinuity, at the cost of requiring five years of history.

input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( ratio( ceq, mul( prcc_f, csho ) ) ), ind_rank( ratio( ratio( che, at ), vol( ratio( add( ib, dp ), at ), 5 ) ) ) )

input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_RANK(RATIO(che, cogs)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Gross-profit-to-price identifies firms priced cheaply against their earning power, but that discount is only collectible by shareholders who are not diluted first; conditioning it on the firm's cash runway should convert a spread that factor models fully explain into one they do not.

A positive result would show the runway channel is portable across valuation legs rather than specific to balance-sheet claims, which would materially generalise the mechanism.

input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_rank( ratio( sub( revt, cogs ), mul( prcc_f, csho ) ) ), ind_rank( ratio( che, cogs ) ) )

input_signals.name: Claim Cheapness With Creditor-Proof Cash
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(SUMRANK(RATIO(SUB(act, lt), MUL(prcc_f, csho)), RATIO(MA(ADD(ib, dp), 3), MUL(prcc_f, csho)))), IND_RANK(RATIO(che, ADD(dltt, dlc))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Two different agents can force a cheap firm to transact before its discount closes — its operations, by consuming cash, and its creditors, by demanding repayment — and cash measured against total interest-bearing debt tests the second channel: a firm that could extinguish its entire debt from cash on hand answers to no lender.
input_signals.reasoning:
Rather than averaging profitability into an existing quality rank, this substitutes a different denominator for the liquidity buffer and thereby separates the two economically distinct forced-transaction risks, so a comparison with the accepted cost-base runway signal identifies which one the alpha actually comes from. Cash-to-debt is not a leverage ratio in disguise because debt-free firms and cash-rich levered firms are ordered by their ability to retire claims outright, and both inputs are universally reported so coverage stays in the high tier.
REASONING_END
